name: Steve Jobs
overview:
Steve Jobs co-founded Apple in his parents' garage in 1976 with Steve Wozniak, was forced out of the company he started in 1985 after a boardroom power struggle, and returned in 1997 to lead one of the most consequential turnarounds in business history. In between, he founded NeXT and bought the computer-graphics division of Lucasfilm for $10 million, renaming it Pixar and steering it toward Toy Story (1995), the first fully computer-animated feature film.

Back at Apple, Jobs presided over a run of products — the iMac, iPod, iPhone, and iPad — that repeatedly redefined their categories and turned Apple into the most valuable company in the world by market capitalization. He was as well known for his uncompromising product sense and design partnership with Jony Ive as for a demanding, sometimes abrasive management style that former colleagues have described in starkly different terms depending on who is telling the story.

Jobs was diagnosed with a rare, initially operable form of pancreatic cancer in 2003 and died in October 2011, two months after resigning as Apple's CEO.
keyAchievements: Co-founded Apple Computer in 1976, then rejoined in 1997 to lead its turnaround from near-bankruptcy to the world's most valuable company
Launched the iMac (1998), iPod (2001), iPhone (2007), and iPad (2010), each of which reshaped its product category
Bought Lucasfilm's computer graphics unit in 1986 and built it into Pixar Animation Studios, sold to Disney in 2006 for $7.4 billion in stock
Pioneered the Apple retail store concept, which became one of the highest-revenue-per-square-foot retail formats in the world
Popularized the graphical user interface for a mass consumer audience via the original Macintosh (1984)

notableQuotes.text: Your time is limited, so don't waste it living someone else's life.
Innovation distinguishes between a leader and a follower.
Design is not just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works.

legacyImpact: Jobs is widely credited with popularizing consumer computing, digital music distribution, and the smartphone-as-computing-platform model that most of the industry now follows. His insistence on tight integration between hardware, software, and design became a template other technology companies have spent two decades trying to replicate. He remains a genuinely contested figure in business biography: several of the products he championed reshaped daily life globally, while his management style is documented (including in Walter Isaacson's authorized biography) as having caused real personal and professional harm to people who worked closely with him — both parts of the record are part of his legacy, not just the product history.
